In this context, the issue revolves around whether gout medications are covered by health insurance.

According to the rules, certain medications such as Allopurinol, Colchicin, and Probenecid are classified as gout medicines. The premise is that if a medication falls under any of these categories, it is considered a gout medicine.

Furthermore, the regulation states that all gout medicines are covered by health insurance. This means that if a medication is classified as a gout medicine, it is automatically eligible for coverage under health insurance.

In conclusion, based on the outlined rules and premises, it can be inferred that gout medicines, including Allopurinol, Colchicin, and Probenecid, are indeed covered by health insurance. This regulation aims to ensure that individuals with gout have access to necessary medications and treatment options.

In the context of social insurance, the question arises whether identification papers can be used as a substitute for identity papers when withdrawing social insurance benefits, specifically lump-sum allowances.

According to Article 109 of the Law on Social Insurance 2014, a dossier for enjoying lump-sum social insurance indemnities must include specific documents, such as social insurance books, the employee's application, and certain identity documents.

In this regard, various identification papers, including ID cards, passports, Citizen Identity Cards, driver's licenses, security badges, airline cards, personal statements, and certifications, can be used as substitutes for identity papers. However, it is essential to note that these documents must meet the specified requirements and be presented in accordance with the regulations.

For instance, passengers holding Vietnamese nationality may present a passport, laissez-passer, permanent/temporary residence card, ID card, or other specified documents to serve as identification. Similarly, employees defined in Article 65 and Clause 5, Article 77 of the Law on Social Insurance 2014 must comply with specific dossier requirements.

In conclusion, identification papers can be used as substitutes for identity papers when withdrawing social insurance benefits, provided they meet the stipulated requirements and are presented in accordance with the relevant regulations.

In the context of business accounting, the issue revolves around whether a company is allowed to hire external accounting services in place of a chief accountant.

According to Clause 3, Article 3 of the Decree, business accounting units, non-state budget-using organizations, and public service providers may hire accounting service providers to act as accountants, chief accountants, or acting chief accountants. This provision aims to provide flexibility and support to these entities in managing their accounting needs.

In the case of a company, it is considered a business accounting unit, which means it has the option to hire external accounting services. This is further supported by the fact that the company's non-availability of a chief accountant or accounting office and hiring of external services, without arranging for a chief accountant or accounting office, is not contrary to the law.

Therefore, based on these regulations, a company is indeed allowed to hire external accounting services in place of a chief accountant, providing it with the necessary support and flexibility to manage its accounting needs effectively.

In the context of employment law, the question revolves around whether employees have a set vacation time in their year.

According to the labor regulations, employees who have worked for an employer for at least 12 months are entitled to annual leave with full pay. If an employee has worked for less than 12 months, the number of annual leave days is proportional to the number of working months.

Employees and employers can negotiate and agree on taking annual leave in installments or in groups for up to every three years. The number of leave days depends on the working time and nature of the job. Employees may also negotiate with their employers about a vacation allowance pool.

Permission to take one vacation per year depends on the agreement between the employee and the employer. The employer must specify the annual leave schedule after consulting the employee and notify them in advance.

In this context, it is clear that employees do not have a fixed or set vacation time in their year. Instead, the number of leave days and the schedule of annual leave are determined by the employment contract, the nature of the job, and the agreement between the employee and the employer.

In this context, the issue revolves around whether morning sickness during pregnancy is covered under the sickness regime.

According to the relevant rules, if a physician or doctor issues a sick leave certificate due to the long duration of pregnancy without any regulation on the convalescence period, the individual is entitled to the sickness regime as prescribed.

In this case, morning sickness is a common symptom experienced by many pregnant women. Although it is not explicitly mentioned in the rules, it can be considered as a health issue related to pregnancy.

Since the rules do not provide a specific regulation on the convalescence period for morning sickness, it can be inferred that morning sickness is not explicitly covered under the sickness regime. However, if a physician or doctor issues a sick leave certificate due to morning sickness, the individual may still be entitled to the sickness regime as prescribed, depending on the specific circumstances and medical evaluation.

In the absence of a clear regulation, it is essential to consult with a healthcare professional to determine the appropriate course of action and entitlement to the sickness regime.

In the context of civil servants, the question arises whether a probation officer is allowed to sign land papers. According to Article 20 of Decree No. 24/2010/ND-CP, persons recruited into civil servants must undergo a probation regime to familiarize themselves with the working environment, practice doing jobs of the working positions recruited, and grasp the provisions of the Law on Cadres and Civil Servants regarding the rights and obligations of civil servants and prohibited acts of civil servants.

During the probation period, the persons recruited to work as civil servants are not yet true civil servants, have not yet independently performed their official duties, and have not been appointed civil servants by the civil servant-managing body. This means that probation officers are still in a transitional phase and do not yet possess the full authority and responsibilities of a civil servant.

In this context, it is clear that a probation officer is not allowed to sign land papers, as they do not have the necessary independence, appointment, or official duty to perform such actions. Signing land papers requires a level of authority and responsibility that is only granted to fully appointed civil servants, not probation officers. Therefore, the conclusion that a probation officer cannot sign land papers aligns with the principles outlined in Article 20 of Decree No. 24/2010/ND-CP.

In the context of land use regulations, the issue revolves around the consequences of using land for improper purposes. According to the law, land users are obliged to use land for proper purposes, within the boundaries of land parcels, and in accordance with regulations on use of depth underground and height above, protection of underground public facilities, and other relevant laws.

If a land user violates these regulations by using land for improper purposes, they will be sanctioned under the law and may even have the land recovered by competent state agencies for land areas used for improper purposes. This means that the State has the authority to take back the land if it is not being used in accordance with the allocated or leased purposes stated in the land use right certificates.

In this case, the conclusion that wrong use of land will be expropriated is not entirely accurate. While land users who violate the law may face sanctions and land recovery, expropriation is a more severe measure that may not be automatically applied in all cases of improper land use. The law provides for a range of measures to address land use violations, and expropriation is just one possible outcome.

It is essential for land users to understand their obligations and responsibilities in using land for proper purposes, within the boundaries of land parcels, and in accordance with relevant regulations to avoid violating the law and facing sanctions or land recovery.

In the context of the Law on Credit Institutions 2010, the question arises whether a finance company must be a joint-stock company.

According to Clause 3, Article 6 of the Law on Credit Institutions 2010, domestic non-bank credit institutions, including finance companies, can be established and organized in the form of either joint-stock companies or limited liability companies. This implies that finance companies have the flexibility to choose their organizational structure.

Moreover, Clause 4, Article 4 of the Law on Credit Institutions 2010 explicitly states that finance companies are non-bank credit institutions. As such, they are subject to the same regulatory requirements as other non-bank credit institutions.

In conclusion, based on the provisions of the Law on Credit Institutions 2010, a finance company does not necessarily have to be a joint-stock company. It can opt to be organized as either a joint-stock company or a limited liability company, depending on its specific needs and circumstances.

In the context of marriage registration involving foreign elements, the dossier required for registration includes various documents and papers. According to Decision No. 299/QD-BTP dated 2016, these documents include passports, ID cards, citizen identity cards, or other documents with photos and personal information issued by competent authorities to prove the identity of Vietnamese citizens.

Additionally, the dossier must include papers proving the place of residence, a marriage registration declaration form with full information on both marriage partners, and a written certification from a Vietnamese or foreign competent health organization that the marriage partners do not suffer from mental diseases or other diseases that render them unable to perceive or control their acts.

In cases where the marital status papers do not indicate an expiry date, these papers and the certification of a medical organization are valid for six months from the date of issue. Furthermore, foreigners and Vietnamese citizens residing overseas must submit copies of their passports or present the originals of passports or passport-substitute papers in case of direct submission of dossiers.

The marital status certificate of a Vietnamese citizen residing in Vietnam is also required, as well as copies of civil status extracts of the recording in registers of their divorce or annulment of illegal marriages, if applicable.

In summary, the dossier for marriage registration involving foreign elements must include a range of documents and papers that prove the identity, place of residence, and marital status of the individuals involved, as well as certifications of their health and capacity to enter into a marriage.

In the context of inheritance law, a will is a statement of an individual's intention to transfer their property to another person after death. For a will to be legally effective, the property must belong to the testator, and the content and form of the will must be valid as prescribed by law.

According to Article 644 of the 2005 Civil Code, certain individuals have the right to inherit property regardless of the will. These include minor children, parents, spouses, and mature children who lack working capacity. However, this provision does not apply to individuals who refuse to receive the estate or are not entitled to inherit under Article 611 of the Code.

In this scenario, the question is whether all the property will be given to the son, and whether others will have a share in it. Based on the laws governing inheritance and wills, the answer is no. The son may not inherit all the property, as other individuals, such as minor children, parents, spouses, or mature children who lack working capacity, may also have a claim to the estate.

Additionally, the testator's will is not the only factor in determining inheritance. The law prioritizes the rights of certain individuals, such as those mentioned above, to inherit property regardless of the will. Therefore, it is possible that others may have a share in the property, and the son may not inherit the entire estate.

In Vietnam, the sale of apartments is subject to personal income tax (PIT) regulations. According to Article 3 of Circular No. 111/2013/TT-BTC and Article 4 of Decree No. 65/2013/ND-CP, individuals who earn income from transferring their houses, land use rights, and property attached to land may be eligible for tax exemption under certain conditions.

To qualify for tax exemption, the individual must have acquired ownership of the house and land use right for at least 183 days prior to the transfer date and must transfer all residential houses and land. However, if these conditions are not met, the income from the transfer is subject to PIT.

Pursuant to Article 23 of the Law on Personal Income Tax 2007 and its amendments in 2012, the total tax rate applicable to income from real estate transfer is 25% of the assessable income. The assessable income is determined by the value of the land use right transfer minus the cost price and relevant reasonable expenses.

In the case of selling apartments, the transfer price is the contractual price, and the cost price of land use right transfer is determined based on the documents on collection of the State's land levies, land rent, or the contracts and lawful documents on payment upon receipt of land-use rights, land-renting rights. Reasonable expenses related to the transfer of land use rights are expenses actually incurred and accompanied with lawful vouchers and invoices.

Therefore, selling apartments is subject to personal income tax, unless the seller meets the conditions for tax exemption.

In the context of company law, the issue at hand is the reissuance of a Certificate of Capital Contribution.

According to the rules, when a member makes a full capital contribution as committed, they are issued a capital contribution certificate. This certificate contains essential information about the company, the member, and the capital contribution. If the original certificate is lost, damaged, or otherwise damaged, the member can be issued another certificate.

In this scenario, the reissuance of the Certificate of Capital Contribution is possible if the original certificate is no longer valid. This is in line with the regulatory principles of ensuring that company records are accurate and up-to-date.

Therefore, it can be concluded that if a Certificate of Capital Contribution is required, it can be reissued if the original certificate is no longer valid, ensuring that the member's capital contribution is properly documented and recognized.

According to Article 4 of Circular No. 14/2020/TT-BCA, the question of whether a partner in jail is allowed to visit revolves around the regulations governing inmate visits. 

In general, inmates are allowed to meet with their relatives, including paternal grandparents, maternal grandparents, natural parents, spouses, natural children, and other family members. Each visit is limited to a maximum of three relatives, but in special cases, the head of the inmate detention center may decide to increase this number to up to five relatives, ensuring that the visit does not compromise the security and safety of the detention facility.

Additionally, representatives from other agencies, organizations, or individuals may also request to meet with an inmate, and the head of the detention center will consider and settle the case if it is deemed appropriate to the lawful interests of the inmates, as well as the requirements of management, education, and rehabilitation of inmates, and crime prevention and combat.

In the context of your question, if your partner is in jail, they are allowed to visit with their relatives, including you, as long as the visit complies with the regulations outlined above. The head of the detention center may also consider special requests or exceptions to these rules, but ultimately, the decision to allow a visit rests with them.

In the context of sex trafficking and purchase, the question revolves around whether engaging in sex trafficking with minors under 18 years old leads to imprisonment.

According to the provided rules, buying sex with minors can be handled according to the provisions of Article 256 of the Penal Code. Specifically, those who have sex with juveniles aged between full 16 years and under 18 years shall be sentenced to between one and five years of imprisonment. Additionally, committing the crime in certain circumstances, such as repeated offenses or causing harm to the victim's health, can lead to imprisonment of between three and eight years.

It is essential to understand that sex trafficking involves the act of paying a sex worker with money or other material benefits to have intercourse, and it is considered a serious offense, especially when it involves minors. The law aims to protect minors from exploitation and abuse, and those found guilty of sex trafficking with minors can face imprisonment.

In conclusion, based on the provided rules, engaging in sex trafficking with minors under 18 years old can lead to imprisonment, as specified in Article 256 of the Penal Code.

In the context of the third drive to reduce electricity prices and bills due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the question arises whether individuals using electricity for daily life are entitled to electricity bill reductions.

According to the rules, entities eligible for assistance in reducing electricity prices and bills include those that engage in business activities, manufacturing sectors, or tourism, as specified in Decision No. 648/QD-BCP and the Law on Tourism 2017. Additionally, facilities serving Covid-19 prevention and control, such as quarantine facilities and healthcare facilities, are also eligible for electricity bill reductions.

However, people using electricity for domestic purposes are specifically excluded from entitlement to electricity price reduction in the third drive due to Covid-19. This means that individuals using electricity for daily life, such as households, are not eligible for electricity bill reductions under this program.

The rules aim to provide targeted support to specific sectors and facilities that are directly involved in Covid-19 prevention and control, while ensuring that the electricity price reduction program is implemented in a fair and controlled manner.

In this context, the question revolves around whether a person living in an extremely disadvantaged area can be issued a health insurance card.

According to Decision No. 103/QD-TTg dated 2019, village Khuôn, White of Ho Đáp Commune, Luc Ngan District of Bac Giang Province is listed as an extremely disadvantaged village of Region III communes. Furthermore, Article 12.3 of Decision No. 103/QD-TTg states that people living in extremely disadvantaged areas are eligible for health insurance contributions from the state budget.

This means that individuals residing in extremely disadvantaged areas, including village Khuôn, White of Ho Đáp Commune, Luc Ngan District of Bac Giang Province, are entitled to receive health insurance cards as prescribed by law. To obtain a health insurance card, one can contact their local People's Committee, which is responsible for making a list of eligible individuals as per the law.

In summary, based on the provided rules and regulations, a person living in an extremely disadvantaged area is eligible for a health insurance card, and they can contact their local People's Committee to initiate the process.

In the context of lending and interest rates, the issue revolves around high-interest lending and its consequences.

According to the 2005 Civil Code, the interest rate of 1.5% in excess of the prescribed interest rate is considered high-interest lending. Additionally, the loan interest rate agreed upon by parties must not exceed 150% of the base interest rate announced by the State Bank for the corresponding loan.

In cases where lenders provide loans at interest rates ten or more times higher than the highest interest rates prescribed by law, with the intention of exploitation, they may be subject to penalties, including fines and imprisonment. Furthermore, those who commit the crime of gaining large illicit profits may face imprisonment and fines.

In this legal context, high-interest lending is considered heavy interest. This means that lenders who engage in high-interest lending practices may be subject to legal consequences, including fines, imprisonment, and other penalties.

It is essential for lenders to comply with the interest rate regulations to avoid legal repercussions and ensure fair practices in the lending industry.

In the context of house leasing, the issue revolves around whether it is possible to sublease land without the land owner's consent.

According to Article 498, subleasing a house to another person without the lessor's written consent is a prohibited act that can lead to the unilateral termination of the lease contract by the lessor. This provision aims to protect the rights of the land owner and ensure that any changes to the lease agreement are made with their knowledge and approval.

In addition, the law explicitly states that it is against the law for a land company to sublease a house to another person without the land owner's consent. This reinforces the importance of obtaining written consent from the land owner before making any changes to the lease agreement.

Therefore, based on these regulations, it is not possible to sublease land without the land owner's consent. The law prioritizes the land owner's rights and interests, and any attempts to sublease without their consent would be considered a violation of their rights.

In this legal context, the issue revolves around the distrainment of corporate assets that are being leased by a third party.

According to the rules, if a third party is holding corporate property, the competent criminal judgment enforcement agency has the authority to issue a decision to distrain such property. This means that the agency can seize the property to enforce a judgment, even if the property is being leased by a third party.

In this scenario, the lessee may continue to lease the property under the signed contract, but the distrainment of the property takes precedence. This is because the enforcement agency's primary goal is to execute the judgment, and the lease agreement does not supersede the agency's authority to distrain the property.

In essence, the conclusion that the corporate property can be distrained, even if it is being leased, aligns with the rules governing judgment enforcement. This ensures that the judgment is executed effectively, while also considering the interests of the lessee.

In the context of obtaining a general aviation business license, the dossier required to request the issue of such a license consists of specific documents and papers.

According to the rules, the dossier must include an application form using Form No. 01, a report detailing the fulfillment of conditions for air transport business, an original copy of the capital certification document, copies from the master register, certified true copies of the articles of association, and the charter capital certificate.

The application form and report are essential components of the dossier, as they provide critical information about the applicant's business plan, organizational structure, and product development strategy. The capital certification document, master register, articles of association, and charter capital certificate serve as supporting documents to verify the applicant's credentials and compliance with regulatory requirements.

In summary, the dossier for requesting a general aviation business license must comprise all these specified documents and papers to ensure a complete and accurate application.

In the context of Vietnam's Labor Code 2019, the issue revolves around the payment of salaries to employees. Specifically, it explores whether it is possible to receive a combined monthly salary and whether salaries can be paid in foreign currency.

According to Article 97 of the Labor Code 2019, employees can receive their salaries in various forms, including hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, piecework, or package wages. The payment schedule and method are agreed upon by the employer and employee, with certain conditions applying to each type of wage.

For instance, employees receiving monthly salaries must be paid once a month or once every half month, with a fixed periodic time agreed upon by both parties. Similarly, those receiving piecework or package wages are paid according to the agreement, with monthly advance wages possible if the work spans multiple months.

In cases where the employer fails to pay salaries on time due to force majeure events, they may delay payment for up to 30 days after taking necessary measures to remedy the situation. If the delay exceeds 15 days, the employer must compensate the employee for the late payment, with interest calculated at the bank's announced rate.

However, the provided rules and goals do not explicitly address the possibility of receiving salaries in foreign currency. The conclusion "all x (Pay(x) -> Monthly(x))" suggests that if an employee receives a salary, it must be a monthly salary, but it does not provide a clear answer to the question of foreign currency payment.

Therefore, based on the available information, it is unclear whether employees can receive salaries in foreign currency. Further clarification or additional regulations may be necessary to determine the answer to this question.

In the context of labor laws, the issue revolves around an employee's entitlement to full-paid leave upon divorce and re-marriage.

According to Article 115 of the Labor Code 2019, employees are entitled to a certain number of days of leave for specific personal and family events, such as marriage, the death of a family member, or the marriage of a child. However, there is no provision in the law that grants full-paid leave for divorce and re-marriage.

In fact, the law only provides for unpaid leave in certain circumstances, and employees may negotiate with their employers for additional unpaid leave. The law does not recognize divorce and re-marriage as events that warrant full-paid leave.

Therefore, based on the current labor regulations, an employee is not entitled to full-paid leave upon divorce and re-marriage.

In the context of Vietnamese law, specifically Article 248 of the 1999 Penal Code, the issue revolves around the criminal liability of individuals engaging in online gambling and winning a prize valued at 20 million dong.

According to Article 248, those who illegally gamble in any form with prizes in cash or kind valued between 2 million dong and under 50 million dong, or under 2 million dong but have already been convicted of this crime or organizing gambling, shall be imposed a fine of between 5 million dong to 50 million dong, subject to non-custodial reform of up to three years or a prison term of between three months and three years.

In this case, since the prize won is valued at 20 million dong, which falls within the specified range, the individual may be held criminally liable for gambling. However, to determine the exact punishment, other factors such as the individual's criminal record, the method of gambling, and the severity of the offense must be considered.

Therefore, based on Article 248 of the 1999 Penal Code, it is possible that the individual may face criminal charges for online gambling, but the specific circumstances of the case will influence the final decision.

In the context of fire prevention and fighting regulations, the question arises whether periodic inspections require prior notice to the inspected entities.

According to the relevant rules, persons in charge of periodical inspections must notify the inspected entities of the time, contents, and composition of the inspectorate at least 03 working days in advance. This notification is crucial in ensuring that the inspected entities are prepared and can assign competent and responsible persons to work with the inspecting person.

Furthermore, the rules stipulate that inspected entities must prepare all necessary information about fire safety inspection as notified and assign responsible persons to work with the inspector upon receipt of the inspection notice.

In light of these regulations, it is clear that prior notice is a necessary condition for periodic inspections of fire prevention and fighting. This allows inspected entities to prepare adequately and facilitates a smooth inspection process. Therefore, the conclusion that periodic inspections require prior notice is a logical and necessary requirement to ensure effective fire safety inspections.

In the context of criminal investigations, the primary concern is maintaining confidentiality and preventing the disclosure of investigation secrets. According to the law, investigators and procurators are required to notify procedure participants and witnesses in advance of their right not to disclose investigation secrets, and this notice must be recorded in writing.

This notification is crucial, as it ensures that those involved in the investigation understand the importance of keeping secrets confidential. Failure to maintain confidentiality can result in criminal liabilities, as outlined in Articles 263, 264, 286, 277, 327, and 328 of the Criminal Code.

Witnesses, in particular, play a vital role in the investigation process. They are invited to participate in investigation activities in specific cases and are accountable for verifying the contents and results of the work performed by investigators in their presence. Their opinions on the matter must be recorded in writing.

In this legal framework, the goal is to prevent the disclosure of investigation secrets in criminal cases. To achieve this, it is essential to ensure that all parties involved in the investigation are aware of their rights and responsibilities regarding confidentiality. By doing so, the integrity of the investigation process is maintained, and the risk of secrets being disclosed is minimized.

In the context of joint-venture agreements, the signing authority is a crucial aspect. According to the law, the joint-venture contract must be signed by the legal representative of the company. However, if the signer is not the legal representative, a written authorization is required.

In this scenario, the question is whether the Deputy General Director of the company is allowed to sign the joint-venture agreement. The answer depends on the company's internal policies and agreements. If the Deputy General Director has been granted written authorization by the legal representative, they can sign the agreement. Otherwise, only the legal representative has the authority to sign the joint-venture contract.

It is essential to note that the law does not regulate the division of work in a joint venture contract, and the specific division shall be as agreed by the parties. This means that the company's internal policies and agreements will determine the signing authority, and the Deputy General Director's role in this context.

In this legal context, the issue revolves around whether parking a vehicle on restricted roads for repairs is subject to an administrative penalty.

According to the regulation, a surprise event is defined as an event where an individual or organization cannot or must not foresee the consequences of their harmful act to society. In such cases, the law enforcement force may consider not imposing an administrative penalty.

However, if a vehicle is parked within the effective zone of a "no parking" sign and the owner is not repairing the vehicle, they may still be subject to an administrative penalty for "driving where there is no parking sign". This implies that parking on restricted roads, even for repairs, is not exempt from penalties if the vehicle is not being actively repaired.

In essence, the regulation aims to maintain public order and safety by restricting parking in certain areas. While repairs may be a legitimate reason for parking, it is essential to ensure that the vehicle is being actively repaired and not simply parked in a restricted area. Therefore, parking a vehicle on restricted roads for repairs may still result in an administrative penalty if the necessary conditions are not met.

According to Article 120 of the Labor Code 2012, employers are required to register their internal working regulations with the provincial labor authority. This registration is a mandatory step to ensure compliance with labor laws and regulations.

The registration process involves submitting an application, which must include a written request, documents concerning labor discipline and material responsibility, a written record of opinions from the representative organization of grassroots-level employees' collective, and the internal working regulations themselves.

 Failure to register internal labor regulations with the provincial labor authority can result in a fine ranging from VND 5,000,010 to VND 10,500,000, as specified in Clause 12, Article 1 of Decree No. 88/2015/ND-CP.

In conclusion, as an employer, it is essential to register your company rules with the provincial labor authority to avoid penalties and ensure compliance with labor laws. This registration is a critical step in maintaining a harmonious and regulated work environment.

In the context of criminal investigations, the issue revolves around the attendance of the victim's family during an autopsy.

According to Article 202 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2015, an autopsy must be conducted by a forensic expert under the chairmanship of an investigator and witnessed by a person. Additionally, procurators must be present to administer the autopsy. The law also allows for the invitation of a criminological expert witness to participate in the autopsy.

However, there is no requirement in the law for the victim's family to be present during the autopsy. In fact, the law only mentions that if exhumation of the body is necessary, the investigation authority shall inform the deceased's relatives. This implies that the family's involvement is limited to being notified in specific circumstances, such as exhumation, rather than being required to attend the autopsy itself.

Therefore, based on the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code 2015, it is not necessary for the victim's family to attend the autopsy in a criminal case. The autopsy is a formal procedure conducted by authorized professionals, and the family's presence is not a legal requirement.

In the context of Vietnamese citizenship, the issue revolves around the validity of a Citizen Identity Card.

According to the relevant regulations, Vietnamese citizens aged 14 years or older are eligible to be granted a Citizen Identity Card, which serves as a personal identification number. The card must be renewed when the citizen reaches specific ages: 25, 40, and 60 years old.

In cases where a citizen's identity card is issued, exchanged, or re-issued within 2 years before the age specified for renewal, the card remains valid until the next renewal age. This provision ensures that citizens do not need to undergo frequent renewal processes.

Based on these rules, it can be concluded that a Citizen Identity Card is generally valid, as long as it has been issued, exchanged, or re-issued in accordance with the regulations and has not reached its renewal age. The card's validity is not affected by the citizen's age, as long as it has been properly obtained and maintained.

In essence, the Citizen Identity Card is a vital document for Vietnamese citizens, and its validity is ensured through a well-structured renewal process that takes into account the citizen's age and the card's issuance or exchange history.

In the context of land use and classification, the question arises whether it is possible to build houses on commercial and service land.

According to Point dd, Clause 2, Article 10 of the 2013 Law on Land, land is classified into three main categories: residential land, agricultural land, and other land. Commercial and service land are further classified as other land.

The law does not explicitly permit or prohibit building houses on commercial and service land. However, it is essential to understand that building houses is a land use purpose, and land use purposes are closely tied to the classification of land.

In this context, it is crucial to note that commercial and service land are not primarily intended for residential purposes. The primary purpose of commercial and service land is to facilitate commercial activities, provide services, or engage in other non-residential uses.

Therefore, based on the land classification and use purposes outlined in the 2013 Law on Land, it is not possible to build houses on commercial and service land. The law prioritizes the original purpose of these land types, which is not residential in nature.

In the context of construction projects, the issue revolves around the expiration and renewal of construction permits. According to the Law on Construction dated 2014, before starting construction, an investor must obtain a construction permit issued by a competent authority, except in cases prescribed in Clause 2 Article 89 of the Law No. 20/2004 on Construction.

A construction permit includes new construction permits, repair and renovation permits, and work relocation permits. The time limit for starting the construction of a work must not exceed 12 months after the date of grant of a construction permit. If the work has not been commenced before the expiration of the construction permit, the investor shall apply for an extension or grant of a new construction permit in accordance with the law.

In this scenario, if a construction permit is about to expire or has expired, the investor has two options: to apply for an extension or to obtain a new construction permit. This ensures that the construction project remains compliant with the relevant laws and regulations.

Therefore, the conclusion that a construction permit can be extended or renewed to avoid expiration aligns with the principles of the Law on Construction, ensuring that construction projects are carried out in a lawful and regulated manner.

In the context of cinematography, the question arises whether a film printing and reproduction establishment can be considered a cinematographic establishment.

According to the definition of cinematography, it is a type of synthetic art that combines moving images with sound, recorded on various materials such as film, magnetic tape, and magnetic discs, for public dissemination through technical means. Cinema activities, including film printing and reproduction, can be carried out in various places, known as cinematographic establishments.

In this case, a film printing and reproduction establishment is indeed a type of cinematographic establishment. This is because the establishment is involved in the process of cinematography, which includes the printing and reproduction of films. The establishment's activities align with the definition of cinematography and cinema activities, making it a part of the broader category of cinematographic establishments.

Therefore, it is possible to conclude that a film printing and reproduction establishment is a cinematographic establishment, as it falls within the scope of cinema activities and cinematography.

In the context of investment and public-private partnerships, the issue revolves around the sectors encouraged to invest in the form of Public-Private Partnerships (PPP).

According to Article 10 of Decree No. 63/2018/ND-CP, the Prime Minister has the authority to decide on other sectors that can be encouraged to invest in PPPs. This means that not all sectors are automatically eligible for PPP investments, but rather, the Prime Minister must make a decision to include them.

Furthermore, PPP investments involve collaboration between public and private entities. This collaboration is essential for PPP investments to be successful, as it brings together the resources and expertise of both public and private sectors.

In this context, the conclusion that all sectors are encouraged to invest in PPPs is not entirely accurate. While the Prime Minister has the discretion to decide on sectors that can invest in PPPs, not all sectors may be eligible or suitable for such investments.

Therefore, it is essential to carefully consider the specific sectors and investments that can benefit from PPPs, as well as the decisions made by the Prime Minister regarding these sectors, to ensure that investments are made in a transparent and effective manner.

In this legal context, the issue revolves around whether an individual is entitled to retrieve their vehicle when the administrative violation record contains a wrong name.

According to Clause 3 and Clause 6 of Article 58 of the Law on Penalties for Administrative Violations 2012, amended by Clause 29 of the amended Law on Penalties for Administrative Violations 2020, an administrative violation record must contain specific information, including the correct name of the violator. If the record contains errors or does not fully and accurately contain the required information, the case must be verified as prescribed in Article 59 of this Law.

In this scenario, if the administrative violation record contains a wrong name, the individual must apply for confirmation of their exact name, address, and permanent residence, and prove that the vehicle is under their ownership. They must then work directly with the party that issued the administrative penalty record to verify the false information during the declaration.

Only after rectifying the incorrect information and completing the necessary verification process can the individual retrieve their vehicle. Therefore, in the presence of a wrong name in the administrative violation record, the individual is not entitled to take back their car until the errors are corrected and the verification process is completed.

In this context, the issue revolves around military conscription and the age at which citizens are called up for service.

According to the laws and regulations, citizens who are 18 years of age shall be called up for military service, and the age of call-up ranges from 18 to 25 years old. However, citizens who have been trained at the college level and have been suspended from call-down are entitled to be called up until the age of 27.

In the case of an 11th-grade student, it is important to note that the age of conscription is not determined by the grade level but rather by the age of the individual. Since the student is still in 11th grade, it is likely that they are below the age of 18, which means they are not yet eligible for conscription.

Therefore, based on the laws and regulations, it is not possible to determine whether an 11th-grade student will be conscripted, as their age is not yet within the range of call-up.

In the context of Vietnamese maritime law, a foreign fishing ship can only operate in Vietnamese waters if it meets certain requirements. 

According to the regulations, a foreign fishing ship must have a certified true copy of the project on cooperation in technical training and transfer of aquatic technology approved by the Minister of Agriculture and Rural Development, as well as a certified true copy of the project of collection and transport of aquatic products approved by Presidents of the People's Committees of provinces and central-affiliated cities. 

Furthermore, the ship must also possess a certified copy of the fishing vessel registration certificate and a certified true copy of the fishing vessel technical safety certificate. 

In essence, a foreign fishing ship cannot operate in Vietnamese waters with an incomplete dossier. The law ensures that only ships that have obtained the necessary approvals and certifications can engage in fishing activities in Vietnamese waters, promoting sustainable fishing practices, and maintaining the integrity of Vietnam's marine ecosystem.

The regulation in question pertains to the responsibilities of the Ministry of Information and Communications in electronic identification and verification, as specified in Article 36 of Decree No. 59/2022/ND-CP.

According to this decree, the Ministry of Information and Communications is responsible for ensuring the use of electronic identities and identity accounts for electronic administrative procedures and public administrative services. The Ministry must also take charge and cooperate with the Ministry of Public Security to provide technical connections, ensuring the security and safety of information within the electronic identification and verification system.

Furthermore, the Ministry of Information and Communications must cooperate with the Ministry of Public Security and the Ministry of National Defense to ensure the overall safety and security of the electronic identification and verification system.

In this context, the Department of Information Technology is not explicitly mentioned as having a specific responsibility in electronic identity and authentication. The regulation primarily outlines the responsibilities of the Ministry of Information and Communications, which may delegate tasks or collaborate with other entities, including the Department of Information Technology, to achieve its objectives.

In essence, the regulation focuses on the Ministry of Information and Communications' role in ensuring the security, safety, and efficiency of electronic identification and verification processes, rather than specifying the responsibilities of the Department of Information Technology.

In the context of advertising regulations, the issue revolves around the penalty for advertising supplements in printed newspapers without separate numbers.

According to the rules, advertising supplements must meet specific requirements to avoid penalties. These requirements include being separately numbered, not being the same size as the main page, and not being issued on the same page of the main newspaper. If these conditions are not met, the publishing entity may be fined.

The fine for non-compliance ranges from 3,000,000 to 5,010,000 VND, as stated in Decree 158/2013/ND-CP. This decree provides guidelines for understanding the regulations and penalties related to advertising supplements in print newspapers.

In essence, the penalty for advertising supplements without separate numbers is a fine within the specified range. This regulation aims to maintain transparency and accountability in advertising practices, ensuring that publishers comply with the necessary standards.

In the context of passport regulations, the issue revolves around the extension of a traveler's passport at a temporary residence.

According to the rules, a traveler's passport is a type of national passport granted to all Vietnamese citizens, valid for a maximum of 10 years from the date of issue, and cannot be extended. Additionally, general passports issued domestically and overseas have the same form and content but with different symbols for management purposes.

In this context, it is not possible to extend a passport at a temporary residence. This is because passports are issued with a specific validity period, and once that period expires, a new passport must be issued rather than extending the existing one. This ensures that passport holders always have a valid travel document, and temporary residences do not have the authority to extend passports.

This regulation is in line with the principles of passport management, which aim to maintain the integrity and security of travel documents. By not allowing passport extensions at temporary residences, the risk of fraudulent activities or unauthorized modifications to passports is minimized, ensuring the safety and security of travelers.

In this legal context, the issue revolves around the punishment for sex trafficking, specifically whether a 16-year-old involved in sex trafficking is subject to an additional fine in addition to imprisonment.

According to the provided rules, those who engage in prostitution of under-18 persons are punishable by law. The punishment varies depending on the circumstances, with imprisonment ranging from one to 15 years. Additionally, offenders may be subject to a fine of between VND 10,000,000 and 50,000,000.

In the case of a 16-year-old involved in sex trafficking, the law does not explicitly state that they are subject to an additional fine. However, since they are under 18 years old, they fall within the scope of the prostitution of under-18 persons. Therefore, they would be punishable by law, including imprisonment and potentially a fine.

It is essential to note that the law aims to protect minors from exploitation and harm. The punishment for sex trafficking is designed to reflect the severity of the offense and to deter others from engaging in such activities.

In conclusion, while the law does not explicitly state that a 16-year-old involved in sex trafficking is subject to an additional fine, they are still punishable by law, including imprisonment and potentially a fine, as part of the overall punishment for engaging in prostitution of under-18 persons.

In the context of emulation and commendation, the question arises whether maternity leave is eligible for consideration for the title of junior emulation soldier.

To address this, we need to examine the criteria for conferring titles such as "Advanced Worker" and "Achievement Fighter". According to Clause 6, Article 1 of the Law on Emulation and Commendation amended in 2013, an individual must discharge assigned tasks with high productivity and quality, comply with Communist Party policies and state laws, demonstrate self-reliance, solidarity, and support, and actively participate in emulation movements. Additionally, they must actively study politics, culture, professional knowledge, and skills, and possess good ethics and a healthy lifestyle.

In this framework, maternity leave is not explicitly mentioned as a factor in determining eligibility for the title of junior emulation soldier. The focus is on an individual's performance, productivity, and quality of work, as well as their adherence to party policies and state laws, and their personal development.

Therefore, based on the provided rules and criteria, it cannot be concluded that maternity leave is eligible for consideration for the title of junior emulation soldier. The emphasis is on an individual's work performance and personal qualities, rather than their leave status.

The question revolves around whether the law requires businesses to pay their employees in March, also known as a bonus. 

According to Article 104 of the Labor Code 2019, a bonus is an amount of money or other forms that an employer gives an employee based on their performance. The reward regulation shall be decided and publicly announced by the employer at the workplace after consulting with the representative organization of employees (if any). 

Notably, the law does not require enterprises to pay wages in March to employees. This means that the decision to pay a bonus in March lies with the employer, and it is not a mandatory requirement under the Labor Code 2019. 

In summary, the law does not obligate businesses to pay their employees in March, and the decision to do so is at the discretion of the employer.

In the context of health insurance coverage, the question arises whether children under 6 years of age treated for strabism eye disease are eligible for health insurance coverage.

According to the regulations, certain medical services and treatments are not eligible for health insurance coverage, such as nursing and convalescence establishments, physical examination, pregnancy testing and diagnosis, assisted reproductive technology, beauty services, and more. However, there are exceptions, like medical examination and treatment, rehabilitation in case of disaster, and the use of medical supplies as alternatives, which are eligible for health insurance coverage.

Specifically, Rule 7 states that treating strabismus, myopia, and refractive errors of the eye is eligible for health insurance coverage, but only for children under 6 years of age. This implies that children under 6 years of age who receive treatment for strabism eye disease are indeed eligible for health insurance coverage.

In conclusion, based on the provided rules and regulations, children under 6 years of age who receive treatment for strabism eye disease are covered by health insurance.

In the context of pesticide trading, the question arises whether a university degree is necessary to sell pesticides.

According to Clause 2, Article 1 of Decree No. 123/2018/ND-CP, pesticide traders must satisfy certain conditions specified in Article 63 of the Law on Plant Protection and Quarantine. One of these conditions is that the person directly managing or selling pesticides must obtain at least an associate degree in plant protection, cultivation, chemistry, biology, or agronomy, or obtain a certificate of completion of a pesticide training course.

This means that a university degree is not required to sell pesticides. Instead, an associate degree or a certificate of pesticide training is sufficient. This regulation aims to ensure that individuals selling pesticides have the necessary knowledge and skills to handle these products safely and effectively.

Additionally, the law also sets out specific requirements for the location and storage of pesticides, including the need for separate storage facilities and adherence to national standards for safety regulations.

In conclusion, a university degree is not necessary to sell pesticides, and an associate degree or a certificate of pesticide training is sufficient to meet the regulatory requirements.

In this legal context, the issue revolves around the eligibility of certain assets to be used as collateral while applying for a construction license and red book.

According to the current law, security assets can include existing assets, future assets, or assets formed from loans, as long as they are not banned from transaction by law. These assets can be in the formulation stage, lawfully created, or registered under law.

In the case of "Rights and benefits arising from investment in projects," which are off-the-plan assets attached to land, registration of secured transactions is required, and a construction permit is also necessary in addition to the application and contract.

The Ministry of Justice's Circular No. 05/2011/TT-BTP provides guidance on registration and provision of information about secured transactions. Furthermore, Circular No. 08/2014/THE MINISTRY OF TRANSFER amends the previous circular.

Receivables, insurance rights, fees collected by the investor, and benefits gained from the trading and exploitation of the value of land use rights or technical infrastructures on land are all considered security assets that require registration of mortgage contracts for secured transactions.

In this context, it is essential to understand that not all security assets can be used as collateral while applying for a construction license and red book. The law requires registration of secured transactions for specific types of security assets, such as those attached to land.

Therefore, without further information about the specific type of security asset and its characteristics, it cannot be concluded whether they are eligible to receive collateral while applying for a construction license and red book.

In the context of contract authentication, the issue revolves around the signing of pages when authenticating a contract.

According to Clause 4, Article 36 of Decree No. 23/2015/ND-CP, the authenticating person is required to write testimonies corresponding to each type of contract according to prescribed forms, sign, specify their full name, and seal of the authenticating agency, and record in the authentication book.

For contracts and transactions with at least two pages, each page must be numbered and signed by both the requester and the authenticating person. The number of pages and testimonies shall be written on the last page of the contract or transaction. Additionally, if the contract or transaction has two sheets or more, the adjoining edges of the contract and transaction sheets must be affixed with overlapping stamps.

In this context, the conclusion that parties sign on the pages when authenticating the contract is a direct result of these regulatory requirements. This ensures that all parties involved in the contract or transaction have acknowledged and agreed to the terms, maintaining the integrity and authenticity of the document.

In this legal context, the issue revolves around the characteristics that define a cult family versus a normal family. According to the rules, a cult family is one that does not comply with community conventions, whereas a normal family is one that flies national flags on national holidays and political events, participates in cultural or artistic activities, practices physical training and sports, and adopts a civilized lifestyle during weddings, funerals, and festivals.

The question is whether not flying the national flag on holidays would earn a family the title of cult family. Based on the provided rules, flying the national flag on national holidays and political events is one of the characteristics of a normal family. Therefore, not flying the flag does not necessarily mean that a family is a cult family.

In fact, there are various ways for a family to be considered normal, such as participating in cultural or artistic activities, practicing physical training and sports, and adopting a civilized lifestyle during important events. As long as a family complies with the law and community conventions, it will not be considered a cult family.

In conclusion, not flying the national flag on holidays does not automatically earn a family the title of cult family. A family's compliance with the law, community conventions, and adoption of a civilized lifestyle are more important factors in determining whether it is a normal family or not.

According to the Law on Social Insurance No. 58/2014, specifically Clause 2, 3, and 4 of Article 31, female employees who give birth to children are eligible for maternity leave under certain conditions.

To be eligible, female employees must have paid social insurance premiums for at least 6 months within 12 months before giving birth or adopting a child. Additionally, if they have paid premiums for the full 12 months or more and take leave for pregnancy care as prescribed by competent medical establishments, they must have paid social insurance for at least 3 months within 12 months before giving birth.

In the case of an employee who takes 8 months of leave 8 months before childbirth, the question is whether she is eligible for maternity leave. Based on the law, the employee must have paid social insurance premiums for at least 6 months within 12 months before giving birth. Since the employee took 8 months of leave, it implies that she did not pay premiums for the required period.

Therefore, according to the law, the employee is not eligible for maternity leave in this scenario.

The issue at hand revolves around the creation of a government entity in relation to the shareholders of a joint-stock company.

According to the relevant law, a joint-stock company is established with a charter capital, which is divided into shares. Shareholders, who can be individuals or organizations, own at least one share of the company. The law stipulates that a joint-stock company must have a minimum of three shareholders, with no maximum limit.

In this context, the goal of creating a government entity with three or more people is not directly related to the establishment of a joint-stock company. The law does not provide a provision for creating a government entity based on the number of shareholders in a joint-stock company.

Therefore, it is essential to distinguish between the legal framework governing joint-stock companies and the process of establishing a government entity. The two are separate and distinct, with different legal requirements and regulations.

In the context of the 2013 Land Law, the issue revolves around whether it is possible to mortgage assets attached to annual leased land to a business.

According to Clause 1 Article 167 of the 2013 Land Law, land users have the right to exchange, transfer, lease, sublease, inherit, donate, mortgage, or contribute land use rights as capital. This means that land users, including organizations, individuals, and establishments, can engage in various transactions related to land use rights.

However, the law does not explicitly allow for the mortgaging of assets attached to annual leased land to a business. The land lease is done through a decision on land lease with annual land rents, land lease, and lump sum land rents for the entire lease period. This implies that the land use rights are tied to the land lease agreement, and mortgaging assets attached to the leased land may not be permitted.

In this case, the conclusion that it is not possible to mortgage assets attached to annual leased land to a business is consistent with the principles of the 2013 Land Law. The law prioritizes the rights of land users and ensures that land use rights are exercised in accordance with the law, which may not include mortgaging assets attached to leased land.

The issue at hand revolves around the identification criteria for poor households in different localities.

According to Article 2 of Decision No. 59/2015/QD-TTg, poor households in rural areas are identified as those with a monthly per capita income of VND 700,000 or less, or those with a monthly per capita income between VND 700,000 and VND 1,000,000 who lack access to at least three basic social services. Similarly, in urban areas, poor households are identified as those with a monthly per capita income of VND 900,000 or less, or those with a monthly per capita income between VND 900,000 and VND 1,300,000 who lack access to at least three basic social services.

The premises highlight that low income and deprivation are key factors in identifying poor households, and that these factors are applicable in both rural and urban areas. The conclusion drawn from these premises is that the criteria for identifying poor households are similar across different localities.

In essence, the decision provides a uniform framework for identifying poor households, taking into account the income and access to basic social services in both rural and urban areas. This ensures that poor households are identified and supported consistently across different regions.

In the context of civil judgment enforcement, the issue revolves around the assignment of enforcers to organize the execution of judgment enforcement decisions.

According to the relevant rules, the head of the civil judgment enforcement agency is responsible for issuing a judgment enforcement decision and assigning an enforcer to organize the execution within specific timeframes, depending on the circumstances. For instance, if a judgment or ruling is received, the head of the agency must issue a judgment enforcement decision and assign an enforcer within 5 working days. Similarly, if a decision on provisional urgent measures is received, the head of the agency must issue a judgment enforcement decision and assign an enforcer within 24 hours.

In general, the assignment of an enforcer is contingent upon the issuance of a judgment enforcement decision. The decision serves as the basis for the enforcement officer to prepare the judgment execution dossier, which must show the entire process of judgment enforcement. The enforcer is responsible for compiling the dossier, recording the work, and retaining all relevant documents.

In this framework, it is essential to understand that the assignment of an enforcer is a crucial step in the judgment enforcement process. The conclusion that the assignment of an enforcer implies the existence of a judgment enforcement decision aligns with the regulatory principles governing civil judgment enforcement activities. This ensures that the enforcement process is carried out in a systematic and transparent manner, with clear documentation and accountability.

It is worth noting that Article 30 of the Law on Enforcement of Civil Judgments in Vietnam (2014) provides that the head of the civil judgment enforcement agency shall issue a judgment enforcement decision and assign an enforcer to organize the execution. This provision further supports the conclusion that the assignment of an enforcer is contingent upon the issuance of a judgment enforcement decision.

In the context of labor laws, the issue revolves around whether holiday vacations are included in the payment of social insurance.

According to the rules, employees are entitled to full paid leave for specific public holidays, and they shall receive full pay during these holidays. However, if an employee does not work and receive a salary for at least 14 working days in a month, they shall not pay social insurance in that month, except for the case of maternity leave.

In this scenario, it is clear that holiday vacations are indeed included in the payment of social insurance. This is because employees receive full pay during public holidays, which implies that they are still receiving a salary. As a result, they are required to pay social insurance during these periods, unless they meet the exception of not working and receiving a salary for at least 14 working days in a month.

This regulation aims to ensure that employees' social insurance contributions are made consistently, even during public holidays when they are not actively working.

In the context of social insurance, health insurance, and unemployment insurance, the question arises whether an enterprise is entitled to suspend unemployment insurance payments due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

According to the relevant regulations, if an employer faces difficulties and has to suspend production and business, they may suspend payment to the retirement and survivorship fund for no more than 12 months. During this suspension period, no inspection of payment or compliance with regulations will be carried out for enterprises affected by the Covid-19 epidemic, provided there are no signs of violations.

However, it is essential to note that enterprises are still required to make full and timely payments to the sickness, maternity, occupational accident, and disease benefit funds, as well as health and unemployment benefit funds, to ensure workers' benefits.

In this scenario, the conclusion that an enterprise is entitled to suspend unemployment insurance due to Covid-19 is not supported. The regulations emphasize the importance of ensuring workers' benefits, even during difficult times, and do not provide a blanket exemption for enterprises to suspend unemployment insurance payments.

In the context of adoption regulations in Vietnam, the question arises whether an overseas Vietnamese adopting a child must pay an adoption registration fee.

According to Article 12 of the Law on Adoption 2010, adoption applicants are required to pay adoption registration fees. Furthermore, Article 6 of the Decree No. 114/2016/ND-CP specifies that the amount of the adoption registration fee is VND 400,000 per case.

However, there are certain cases where exemption or reduction of adoption registration fees may be applicable, as outlined in Article 4 of the Decree No. 114/2016/ND-CP. These cases include step-parents adopting step-children, natural aunts or uncles adopting nieces or nephews, disabled children, children infected with HIV/AIDS or fatal diseases, and people with meritorious services to the revolution adopting children.

In the case of an overseas Vietnamese adopting a child, they are considered Vietnamese citizens and are therefore subject to the same adoption registration fee requirements as domestic Vietnamese citizens. Unless they fall under one of the exempted categories, an overseas Vietnamese adopting a child would be required to pay the adoption registration fee.

In conclusion, based on the provided legal context, an overseas Vietnamese adopting a child would typically be required to pay an adoption registration fee, unless they meet the specific exemption criteria outlined in the relevant regulations.

In the context of inheritance law, the issue revolves around whether stepchildren can inherit from their stepfather and whether the court can be requested not to divide the estate.

According to Article 654 of the 2015 Civil Code, stepchildren and stepfathers or stepmothers can inherit each other's estate if they have a relationship of care and nurturing similar to that of a biological father and mother. This means that stepchildren can inherit from their stepfather, but only if they have a close and caring relationship.

However, the court's role in dividing the estate is not explicitly mentioned in the article. In general, the court's primary function is to ensure that the inheritance process is carried out in accordance with the law and the wishes of the deceased.

In this case, the conclusion that stepchildren can request the court not to divide the estate is not supported by the provided legal context. The court's decision on estate division is typically based on the applicable laws and the specific circumstances of the case, rather than on a request from the stepchildren.

Therefore, while stepchildren may be eligible to inherit from their stepfather under certain conditions, the court's decision on estate division is a separate matter that depends on the relevant laws and the specific facts of the case.

In the context of assisted reproductive technology, specifically artificial insemination, the question arises as to whether a husband is obligated to support a child born through this method in the event of divorce.

According to Clause 21, Article 3 of the relevant law, birth with assisted reproductive technology refers to the birth of a child through artificial insemination or in vitro fertilization.

In the case of artificial insemination, the identification of parents is governed by Article 92, which states that the identification of parents shall comply with the provisions of Article 88 of this Law. Article 88 stipulates that children born during the marriage period or conceived by the wife during the marital period are considered common children of the husband and wife.

Furthermore, Clause 2 of Article 82 of the law emphasizes that fathers and mothers who do not directly raise their children have the obligation to support them.

In this scenario, since the child is born through artificial insemination, which is considered a common child of the husband and wife, the husband has a legal obligation to support the child, even in the event of divorce. This obligation is rooted in the principle that both parents are responsible for the well-being and upbringing of their child, regardless of their marital status.

Therefore, the conclusion that a husband must support a child born through artificial insemination in the event of divorce aligns with the provisions of the relevant law, ensuring the child's welfare and upholding the responsibilities of both parents.

In the context of traffic regulations, the question arises whether the traffic police have the authority to sanction vehicles running through irrigation works.

According to the rules, chiefs of district-level police authorities, captains of the Marine Police, and heads of specialized divisions of the Traffic Police Department, including heads of waterway police departments and Traffic Police departments, have the power to impose fines for administrative violations related to disaster preparedness, operation, and protection of hydraulic structures and flood control systems.

Specifically, the Head of the Traffic Police Department has the power to impose penalties for violations against regulations on operating an overloaded vehicle through a hydraulic structure. This implies that the traffic police have the authority to sanction vehicles running through irrigation works, as they are responsible for enforcing regulations related to the operation and protection of hydraulic structures.

In essence, the traffic police have the power to sanction vehicles that violate regulations related to hydraulic structures, including irrigation works. This power is granted to ensure compliance with traffic regulations and maintain public safety.

In this legal context, the issue revolves around the entitlement of a Commune military deputy commander to receive social insurance benefits when resigning from their position.

According to the relevant regulations, individuals who have worked continuously for at least 60 months and are absent from social insurance are eligible to receive a lump-sum allowance when leaving their job. The amount of this allowance is calculated based on the average allowance of the last 60 months, with adjustments made for odd months of service.

However, the specific circumstances of the Commune military deputy commander's resignation are not explicitly addressed in the provided rules. The rules primarily focus on the general conditions for receiving social insurance benefits, such as continuous work and absence from social insurance.

In the absence of explicit provisions, it is unclear whether the Commune military deputy commander is entitled to receive social insurance benefits when resigning. Further clarification or additional information is needed to determine their eligibility for these benefits.

It is essential to consult relevant laws and regulations governing social insurance for military personnel and government officials to resolve this issue. The specific circumstances of the Commune military deputy commander's resignation and their employment history will likely play a crucial role in determining their eligibility for social insurance benefits.

In the context of promotional programs of chance, the issue revolves around the requirement to notify the Department of Industry and Trade about the evidence for determining prize winners.

According to the rules, the determination of prize winners must be publicly organized, witnessed by customers, and recorded in writing, following the announced rules. Additionally, if prize-winning proofs are issued together with goods, traders conducting sales promotion must notify the provincial-level Industry and Trade Departments of the locality where the proofs are issued before the issuance.

In this case, the conclusion that the evidence for determining promotion prize winners by chance requires notification to the Department of Industry and Trade is not supported. The rules do not explicitly require notification to the Department of Industry and Trade for all cases of determining prize winners. The notification requirement only applies when prize-winning proofs are issued together with goods, and even then, it is limited to notifying the provincial-level Industry and Trade Departments of the locality where the proofs are issued.

Therefore, the evidence for determining promotion prize winners by chance is not necessarily required to be notified to the Department of Industry and Trade in all cases. The rules provide specific guidelines for notification, and not all prize determinations fall under these guidelines.

In the context of intellectual property law, the issue revolves around when copyright arises for a created work.

According to Clause 1, Article 6 of the 2005 Intellectual Property Law, copyright arises from the moment a work is created and expressed in a certain material form, regardless of its content, substance, form, medium, language, publication, or registration status. This means that copyright is not dependent on whether the work is registered or published, but rather on the fact that it has been created and expressed in a tangible form.

In other words, the act of creating a work and expressing it in a material form is what gives rise to copyright, not the date of registration. The registration or publication of a work may provide additional legal benefits, but it is not a prerequisite for copyright to exist.

Therefore, the conclusion that copyright arises from the date of registration is incorrect. Instead, copyright arises from the moment of creation and expression of a work in a material form, as stated in the 2005 Intellectual Property Law.

In the context of corporate income tax, the question arises whether a loss on capital transfer can be considered a deductible expense.

According to Clause 1 Article 7 of Circular No. 78/2014/TT-BTC, income from capital transfer or securities transfer is subject to corporate income tax. Furthermore, Point b Clause 2 Article 14 of Circular No. 78/2014/TT-BTC states that income from capital transfer is considered another income and must be declared as taxable income when calculating corporate income tax.

In addition, Clause 9 Article 18 of Circular No. 78/2014/TT-BTC provides that if an enterprise suffers losses in the same tax period, it can offset those losses against taxable incomes from profitable activities. If the enterprise cannot separate losses from each activity, it may transfer the losses to income from activities eligible for enterprise income tax incentives first, then to income from activities ineligible for enterprise tax incentives.

In this case, since the loss on capital transfer is considered taxable income, it can be offset against other taxable incomes of the enterprise. Therefore, the loss on capital transfer can be included as a deductible expense. This is in line with the tax regulations, which aim to ensure that enterprises accurately report their income and losses for tax purposes.

In the context of labor laws, the issue revolves around whether a female employee who has given birth to twins can return to work before the end of her maternity leave period.

According to the law, a female employee can work before the end of her maternity leave period if she meets certain conditions. These conditions include taking leave for at least 4 months and obtaining prior notice and consent from her employer.

However, in the case of twins, the law does not provide a specific exemption or exception to these conditions. Therefore, a female employee who has given birth to twins must still meet the same conditions as any other female employee to return to work before the end of her maternity leave period.
